rationale: When step 7 (code coverage collection) fails, we apply the 'fresh' policy: delete the failed sandbox entirely and provision a new one with a unique name. This trades cost (a new boot) for simplicity and reliability — there is no risk of corrupted state from the failed step bleeding into the retry. The 'resume' policy would be cheaper but risks resuming with a half-written coverage database. The 'rollback' policy requires a pre-step-7 snapshot, which adds overhead to every run. For short-lived autograder jobs (< 2 min), 'fresh' is the right tradeoff: cost is minimal and correctness is guaranteed. In production we would use 'rollback' for long (> 10 min) jobs where the cost of re-running all prior steps exceeds the snapshot storage cost.
